name: Passkeys and WebAuthn sign in
plain: Phishing resistant sign in with a key stored on the device or password manager.
meaning: The site gets a public key, a credential ID, a user handle and a signed challenge, not a secret. Attestation is usually withheld so the device model is not revealed. FIDO Alliance said in 2025 that over 15 billion accounts could use passkeys.

access.prompt_ui: Browser or OS prompt for passkey with biometric or PIN
access.persistence: Credential lives in the authenticator until deleted; syncs through iCloud Keychain or Google Password Manager
access.revocation: Clear site data, browser privacy settings

limits.headline: Can sign you in with a passkey after your fingerprint, face or PIN
limits.user_action: You tap Sign in with a passkey and confirm with your fingerprint, face or PIN
can: Ask your device or password manager to prove it holds your passkey
Receive a public key, a credential ID and a signed answer for that site
Sign you in on later visits without you typing a password
Offer your passkey from a nearby phone or a synced password manager
cannot: Get your fingerprint, face or the private key; these never leave your device
Use your passkey on a different site; each passkey is tied to one site name
See which phone or laptop model you have, because that detail is usually withheld
Sign you in without your approval each time
limits.differs: Chrome, Safari, Edge and Firefox all support it. Where passkeys are stored and synced depends on iCloud Keychain, Google Password Manager or another manager.

story.what_it_is: Sign in with your face, finger or device PIN instead of a password. Nothing secret is sent.

marketing.name: Passkeys
marketing.pitch: Apple sells passkeys as a safer, easier replacement for passwords, unlocked with Face ID or Touch ID and synced through iCloud Keychain.

marketing.name: Passkeys
marketing.pitch: Google pitches passkeys as sign in with your fingerprint, face or screen lock, and says they resist phishing.

marketing.name: Passkeys
marketing.pitch: The standards group describes passkeys as a simpler and stronger way to sign in than passwords.

story.for_you: You tap the username box, pick your account from a small list, and unlock with your face, fingerprint or screen PIN. No password to remember. A fake copy of the site cannot trick you into handing anything over.
story.for_makers: Passkeys cut password reset support costs and stop phishing and password reuse attacks. Sites also see higher sign in success and fewer account takeovers, which helps both revenue and trust.

use_cases.example: A player opens a console or game account page on the web and signs in with a passkey, so a stolen password can no longer steal their skins and purchases.
A cloud gaming site such as Xbox Cloud Gaming lets a person sign in with their Microsoft passkey on a borrowed laptop, then streams a game within a minute.
A bank website lets a customer approve sign in with a fingerprint on their laptop, with no text message code to intercept.
A shopper checks out on a phone and unlocks the saved account with Face ID, without typing a password on a tiny keyboard.
A work web app such as an online editor or code host signs people in with a passkey stored in their password manager, synced across laptop and phone.
A fraud team counts how many accounts are protected by passkeys and treats a passkey sign in as strong proof that the real owner is present.
A payments page asks for a quick passkey check before a large transfer, adding proof it is really you.

risks: Lock in to one device ecosystem

technical_bounds: Site never sees the private key
Origin bound: works only on the registered domain

abuse: Tying an account to a device when attestation is shared

history.change: WebAuthn Level 1 became a W3C Recommendation
Passkeys in Google Password Manager across devices
